items.answer: Not settled. Sovereignty discount cost is an informal umbrella term that the paper does not operationalise or estimate. The simulator's cost proxy is unitless, omits institutional overheads, and is not compared against laboratory settings.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: there is no estimate of sovereignty discount cost and the cost proxy is unitless and excludes institutional overheads, so no comparison is made.

items.question: Does the paper show that a 20% human-audit budget is sufficient to keep a strategic model safe? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper draws no quantitative conclusions from the run. Its only strategic agent is scripted and far weaker than a capable red team. The paper also cites work showing that attack selection can substantially degrade safety at realistic audit budgets.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: no quantitative conclusions are drawn and the scripted agent cannot stand in for a capable adversary (and cited work warns about attack selection).

items.question: Does the paper show that compute governance and deployment-time AI control should be merged into a single framework for regulated deployers? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper notes that the two literatures operate at different levels and rarely address each other. It explicitly declines to attempt a synthesis, mentioning them only to situate regulated deployers, who are affected by both.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: the paper explicitly does not attempt a synthesis and only notes the two conversations.

items.question: Does the paper show that well-calibrated output-level trusted monitoring alone would give the Operator adequate oversight assurance? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The paper says no single protocol should be presented to a board or regulator as a complete answer. Monitoring also has value only if flags are acted on through staffed review and incident processes, and evaluation must cover diagnosis, usefulness and cost as well as prevention.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Reason: the paper states that no single protocol is a complete answer and that monitoring needs action and review processes (and multi-dimensional evaluation).

items.question: Does the paper show that the data-colonialism account of AI asymmetries is correct? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper uses the structural-asymmetry literature narrowly, to motivate treating the position of AI-importing jurisdictions as persistent. It explicitly does not advance a normative theory of colonialism or adjudicate broader moral claims.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: the literature is used only narrowly to motivate persistence of the importing position, and the paper explicitly declines to adjudicate the theory.

items.question: The pre-execution gateway is treated as an architectural element of the deployer's own application. Would it provide any prevention for a deployer whose vendor-hosted agent executes tool calls directly against internal systems, without passing through the deployer's application, and why?
items.answer: No. The gateway works by holding, replacing, escalating or passing a recommended action at a point between recommendation and execution inside the deployer's own application. If execution bypasses that application, there is no point at which the gateway can intervene. Interaction access depends on the deployer's own application architecture.
rubric: Concludes the gateway would provide little or no prevention in this setup
Reasons that the gateway can only act (hold/replace/escalate/pass) at a review step between recommendation and execution located in the deployer's application, which is bypassed here
Notes that interaction-layer control depends on the deployer's own application architecture or routing

items.question: The macro-shutdown protocol escalates or puts clusters into safe mode after repeated suspiciousness. When would it fail to stop a C2 pattern like the stress scenario's slow elevation in hold recommendations, and why?
items.answer: It fails when the per-case monitor does not score the individual biased recommendations as suspicious, because each one looks plausible on its own. Macro-shutdown only triggers on accumulated suspicious signals. Without them, the mis-triage keeps propagating across many cases before it is detected.
rubric: Identifies the failure condition as individual recommendations not being flagged or scored as suspicious by the monitor
Reasons that macro-shutdown depends on repeated suspiciousness signals, so a pattern made of individually unflagged cases never triggers it and propagates (the C2 harm)

items.question: Suppose the Operator secures the 'notified' model-version-control setting rather than 'pinned'. When would this fail to preserve the validated status of the model the Operator relies on, and why?
items.answer: It fails when the Operator lacks the capacity to revalidate before or promptly after the notified change takes effect. Notification only tells the Operator that the vendor-held model is changing on the vendor's schedule; it does not stop the change. Whether the notice protects anything depends on absorptive capacity: staff able to re-run validation and monitoring.
rubric: Identifies the failure condition as the Operator lacking capacity to revalidate or re-monitor in time (or the change proceeding regardless)
Reasons that 'notified' informs the Operator but does not stop the model changing on the vendor's schedule, so it protects validation only if the Operator can act on it (absorptive capacity)

items.question: With tool-call logs set to partial, when would the tool monitor protocol leave C3-type exposures unscored, and why?
items.answer: It would miss them when the tool calls that expose sensitive fields fall outside the partially logged portion. The tool monitor can only score tool or action use where tool visibility exists. In the case, C3 is defined as exposure through tool calls or outputs, so unlogged calls are a blind spot.
rubric: Identifies the condition as the exposing tool calls not being among those captured by partial logging
Reasons that the tool monitor scores only tool use that is visible to it, and C3 can arise through tool calls

items.question: Against the stealthy access-aware agent, when would raising the human audit protocol's budget from 2% to 20% fail to improve safety much, and why?
items.answer: It would help little when monitoring is weak. In that condition the stealthy agent picks lower-visibility failure modes that are not flagged. The human audit protocol reviews only flagged cases, so a larger budget just reviews more of the wrong, or innocuous, flagged cases. Audit capacity is only as good as the flags that feed it.
rubric: Identifies weak monitoring (the agent's failures not being flagged) as the condition
Reasons that human audit only reviews flagged cases and the stealthy agent chooses lower-visibility failures when monitoring is weak, so extra audit budget does not reach them

items.question: For what kind of jurisdiction would the paper's reason for setting aside Position B in favour of Position C stop holding, and why?
items.answer: It stops holding for a jurisdiction that can actually make full-stack capability investments on the relevant timescale: domestic models, compute and control. The paper sets B aside only because it is not actionable this decade for many states, not because it is wrong. Where B is actionable, that rationale lapses.
rubric: Identifies a jurisdiction able to build full-stack sovereign capability (domestic models, compute, control) on relevant timescales
Reasons that Position C was adopted because B is not actionable for many states, not because B is shown wrong

items.question: When would even a well-drafted guaranteed vendor-support tier stop giving the Operator reliable diagnosis support, and why?
items.answer: It stops when the vendor, or a state actor behind the supply, revokes, degrades or modifies the terms of supply, for example because supply becomes tied to political alignment as with Pax Silica. Arrangements that depend on vendor cooperation are subject to change. Contracts also cannot specify all contingencies.
rubric: Identifies the condition as supply terms being revoked, degraded or changed by the vendor or a state actor (e.g., politically conditioned supply)
Reasons that vendor-dependent arrangements are fragile and change-prone, and/or that contracts are incomplete

items.question: Why is tool scope classed as a 'deployment design substitute' rather than assigned to one of the four sovereignty layers like the other experimental factors?
items.answer: Restricting tool scope requires no access to the model, its traces or vendor support. The deployer can do it in its own workflow design. It substitutes for missing visibility and control by removing risky actions outright instead of detecting them.
rubric: States that scope restriction does not depend on access to any stack layer (model, infrastructure, etc.) but is something the deployer can do in its own design
Explains it substitutes for missing oversight access by removing risky actions rather than monitoring or diagnosing them

items.question: Why does the paper expect reliance on vendor attestations to increase contract-management effort even as it reduces internal validation effort?
items.answer: The attestations have to be secured and enforced through contract. Audit and attestation provisions, change-notification and incident clauses all sit in the contractual spend category, and they need negotiation and ongoing management. So the oversight work moves from the validation budget line to the contract-management line rather than disappearing.
rubric: Explains that attestations must be obtained through contractual provisions (audit/attestation clauses) that need negotiation and management
Links this to the paper's cost-shifting view: effort moves between budget lines rather than being eliminated

items.question: Why does the environment model vendor support as a configurable setting (none, delayed, guaranteed) rather than assuming a single fixed level?
items.answer: Under the paper's incomplete-contracting and bargaining-power view, vendor support depends on the terms negotiated. Vendor concentration varies, and contracts cannot cover every contingency. Different deployers will therefore end up with very different support levels, and protocols like vendor escalation depend on those terms.
rubric: Explains that vendor support depends on negotiated terms that vary with bargaining power or vendor concentration and incomplete contracts
Notes that protocols relying on vendor support (e.g., vendor escalation) therefore vary in usefulness with those terms

items.question: Why would evaluating the environment's protocols with only the honest agent fall short of what the AI control framework requires?
items.answer: Control is evaluated against a worst-case, deliberately subversive model, not just against routine mistakes. The honest agent only gives a baseline of ordinary error. Protocol performance against strategic behaviour that exploits weak monitoring would go untested. That is why the stealthy access-aware agent is included, even though it is crude.
rubric: States that AI control requires safety against a worst-case or strategic untrusted model, not only ordinary errors
Explains the honest agent only represents ordinary error, so strategic exploitation would be untested

items.question: Why do results showing that untrusted monitoring needs explicit collusion-strategy assumptions to support a safety case lend support to Position A?
items.answer: Position A holds that a protocol a deployer cannot fully verify should not count as safety assurance. If a monitoring safety case rests on collusion assumptions that cannot be verified, a deployer cannot confirm the protocol works as intended. That is exactly the verifiability gap Position A objects to.
rubric: States Position A's criterion: protocols that cannot be fully verified should not count as safety assurance
Explains that unverifiable collusion assumptions make the monitor's assurance unverifiable, fitting A's objection

items.question: Why does the Operator's contractual spend need to include regulator-access provisions?
items.answer: The regulator expects documented validation, monitoring and auditability for material models. But the model, its documentation and the serving operations are vendor-held. Supervisory examination of the system therefore depends on contractual rights for the regulator to reach vendor information.
rubric: Notes the regulator's expectations of auditability and supervision of material models
Explains that because the model and serving are vendor-controlled, regulator access must be secured by contract

items.question: Under the Operator's access arrangement in the case, could the Operator implement a pre-execution gateway in-house?
items.answer: Yes. The gateway is a review step within the deployer's own application, and the interaction layer is operator-led. The Operator designs and runs the surrounding application, workflow and tool interfaces.
rubric: Answers yes
Reasons that the gateway sits in the deployer's own application and the Operator leads the interaction layer (application, workflow, tool interfaces)

items.question: Under the Operator's access arrangement in the case, could the Operator implement weights escrow or patching in-house?
items.answer: No. The model layer is vendor-led and weights are vendor-held under managed-endpoint access. Weights patching is typically handled through vendor processes.
rubric: Answers no
Reasons that weights are vendor-held or the model layer is vendor-led, so patching goes through the vendor

items.question: Does the large run's configuration set allow the paper to attribute differences in diagnosis success to the trace-access setting?
items.answer: No. The 20 access profiles are curated, not full-factorial, so trace access varies together with other settings. The simplified protocols were also not designed for causal identification.
rubric: Answers no
Reasons that the curated, non-full-factorial configurations confound settings and do not support causal attribution

items.question: Does the large run allow the paper to claim that the environment produces the diagnosis-success metric for every access configuration it covers?
items.answer: Yes. The run completed all 27,000 condition rows and produced the full metric set, including diagnosis success, for every row. That is the kind of execution claim the run is designed to support.
rubric: Answers yes
Reasons that all condition rows completed with all metrics produced, which is a tooling or execution claim rather than a causal one

items.question: Could the paper's four-layer access typology be used to describe a hospital's deployment of a vendor model?
items.answer: Yes. The descriptive framework is sector-agnostic and is offered as an aid for any regulated deployer's position across data, model, infrastructure and interaction.
rubric: Answers yes
Reasons that the descriptive framework is sector-agnostic

items.question: Could the payments case's C1–C4 catastrophic-action classes be adopted directly as a hospital deployment's catastrophic-action classes?
items.answer: No. The C1–C4 classes are specific to payments: holds, mis-triage, financial data and settlement. The case interpretation is not sector-agnostic, and healthcare may have fuzzier catastrophes and wider action surfaces.
rubric: Answers no
Reasons that the classes are payments-specific and the case is not sector-agnostic, with other sectors having fuzzier catastrophes or wider action surfaces

items.question: Under the paper's cost-shifting observation, is narrowing an AI assistant's scope expected to increase manual-processing effort?
items.answer: Yes. The paper's example is that narrowing scope may reduce monitoring effort but increase manual processing. The work the model no longer does has to be done by people.
rubric: Answers yes
Reasons with the cost-shifting example that excluded work moves to manual processing

items.question: Under the paper's cost-shifting observation, is narrowing an AI assistant's scope expected to increase monitoring effort?
items.answer: No. The paper expects narrowing scope to reduce monitoring effort, because fewer, less risky actions need to be watched. The cost reappears elsewhere, as manual processing.
rubric: Answers no (it is expected to reduce monitoring effort)
Reasons that there are fewer risky actions to monitor and the cost shifts to other lines such as manual processing

items.question: A user reruns the large-run configuration but keeps only the stealthy access-aware agent and only the 20% audit budget, leaving everything else unchanged. How many condition rows and case simulations result?
items.answer: The calculation is 20 profiles × 10 protocols × 1 agent × 3 thresholds × 1 audit budget × 5 seeds = 3,000 condition rows. At 50 cases per condition, that gives 150,000 case simulations.
rubric: Gives 3,000 condition rows
Gives 150,000 case simulations (3,000 × 50)

items.question: A deployer has very few staff able to review flagged cases but generous latency and compute budgets. Between resampling and output monitoring with human audit, which fits its constraints better, and why?
items.answer: Resampling fits better. Its main regulated-deployer consideration is cost and latency, which this deployer can absorb. Human audit depends on staffing and escalation capacity, which it lacks. Even so, resampling should not be presented as a complete answer.
rubric: Chooses resampling
Reasons that resampling's constraint is cost or latency (available here) whereas human audit's is staffing or escalation (scarce here)
Optionally notes no single protocol is a complete answer

items.question: A deployer's vendor product tier provides only partial input/output logs. Which layer of the typology does this affect, which instruments could improve it, and which outcome dimension is most at risk?
items.answer: It affects the interaction layer. That layer can be improved through product tier or contract terms, or by having the deployer's own application architecture record prompts, outputs and tool calls. Diagnosis, meaning the ability to reconstruct failures after the fact, is most at risk.
rubric: Identifies the interaction layer
Names product tier/contract and/or the deployer's own application architecture as levers
Identifies diagnosis or after-the-fact reconstruction as the dimension most at risk

items.question: A bank deploys a well-calibrated output monitor, but its regulator has little experience interpreting AI monitor outputs or challenging vendor attestations. What does the balancing framework imply about supervisory oversight here, and what remedy does it point to?
items.answer: The absorptive-capacity consideration applies to the regulator as well as the deployer. Oversight is only useful if it can be exercised, so supervisory oversight will be weak despite the good monitor. Coalition paths such as regional regulatory colleges could pool and amortise the needed capability.
rubric: Concludes supervisory oversight is limited because the absorptive-capacity consideration covers the regulator too
Points to coalition paths (e.g., regional regulatory colleges or shared arrangements) as a remedy

items.question: A deployer considers making a newly proposed control protocol, backed by a single recent study, a central pillar of its oversight. What does the balancing framework advise, and why?
items.answer: It advises placing limited reliance on the protocol and combining it with better-established controls. The protocol-maturity consideration says reliance should track the evidence base, and a single recent study is thin. Because control recommendations evolve, the deployer would also struggle to justify the choice to validators over multi-year horizons.
rubric: Advises limited reliance (or not making it central)
Reasons via protocol maturity: reliance should match the evidence base, which is thin here
Optionally notes evolving research complicates multi-year justification

items.question: A vendor pitches a built-in monitor that flags nearly all unsafe outputs. Which two of the paper's recurring distinctions does this claim leave unaddressed for a regulated deployer?
items.answer: First, it leaves open monitoring versus acting on monitoring: flags have value only if the deployer has staff and a process to handle them. Second, it leaves open detecting versus explaining: flagging does not show whether failures can be traced to their origin for post-incident review.
rubric: Names monitoring vs acting on monitoring, with the point that flags need a handling process or staff
Names detecting vs explaining, with the point that flagging does not provide diagnosis or post-incident reconstruction

items.question: If the control tax as priced by Terekhov et al. had already included procurement, legal review and vendor-management frictions, which part of the paper's decomposition would lose its rationale as a separate term?
items.answer: The sovereignty discount cost would lose its rationale as a separate term. It is added to the instrumented-control cost precisely to capture the institutional overheads that protocol-level pricing (monitoring, auditing, the safety-usefulness trade-off) leaves out.
rubric: Identifies the sovereignty discount cost term
Explains it exists to capture institutional frictions omitted from protocol-level control-tax pricing

items.question: If a deployer could readily switch between many substitutable frontier-model vendors, which parts of the paper's normative discussion would lose much of their force?
items.answer: Two parts would weaken. The vendor-concentration and bargaining-power consideration would matter less. Position B's argument that foreign-dependent arrangements are fragile, because a supplier can revoke or degrade terms, would also lose force, since switching would blunt any single supplier's leverage.
rubric: Names the vendor concentration/bargaining power consideration
Names Position B's fragility or revocation argument as weakened, because substitutability limits a supplier's leverage

items.question: If the environment's stealthy access-aware agent were replaced by a capable LLM red team, which caveat about the run's outputs would weaken, and which would still prevent treating them as real-world evidence?
items.answer: The caveat against drawing adversarial-robustness conclusions from a scripted, weak agent would weaken. But the outputs would still not be real-world evidence. The data and workflow are synthetic, configurations are curated rather than full-factorial, and human factors and institutional overheads are not modelled.
rubric: Identifies the adversarial-robustness caveat (scripted agent far weaker than a red team) as weakened
Names at least one remaining barrier: synthetic data or workflow, curated non-factorial configurations, or unmodelled human/institutional factors

items.question: If the environment's latency proxy were removed, which practical concern about a specific protocol in the payments case could the environment no longer represent?
items.answer: It could no longer represent the cost-and-latency concern about resampling. Additional queries affect throughput and service levels, and dispute-handling timelines are set by scheme rules or regulation. Without a latency measure, resampling's main regulated-deployer drawback would be invisible.
rubric: Identifies resampling's cost/latency concern
Links it to service levels or dispute-handling timelines set by scheme rules or regulation

items.question: If the Operator's tool set could not be narrowed (for example, because the vendor's agent exposed fixed tools), which elements of the paper would lose support?
items.answer: Three elements would lose support. Scope decisions, meaning excluding C4-adjacent paths and constraining tools, would stop being an available spend category and lever. The claim that payments is favourable terrain partly because tool surfaces can be narrowed would weaken. Scope restriction as a practical protocol for the case would also go.
rubric: Names the scope-decisions spend category or scope restriction lever as lost
Names the favourable-terrain reason that tool surfaces can be narrowed as weakened

items.question: If the Operator's vendor refused any change-notification clause, which environment setting would represent the Operator's situation, and which case requirement would be put under strain?
items.answer: The model-version-control setting 'unpinned' would represent the situation, because the model changes on the vendor's schedule without notice. This would strain the model risk function's practice of validating a specific model and monitoring it for drift, including the periodic revalidation the case expects.
rubric: Identifies the 'unpinned' model-version-control setting
Identifies strain on validation of a specific model, drift monitoring or revalidation by the model risk function

items.question: Does the paper show that import-dependent regulated deployers typically lead their own interaction layer? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The typology says interaction access varies with product tier, contract and the deployer's application architecture. The operator-led finding comes from a single illustrative, anonymised case, not from a survey of deployers.
rubric: Answers not settled
Reasons that the typology says interaction access varies with product tier, contract and architecture, and the operator-led result is from one illustrative case

items.question: Does the paper show that resampling is unsuitable for payments-dispute workflows? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper only flags cost and latency questions against service levels and scheme-rule timelines, which a deployer must weigh. The environment's results are not used to draw quantitative conclusions about any protocol.
rubric: Answers not settled
Reasons that the paper raises cost/latency considerations without a verdict and draws no quantitative protocol conclusions from the simulation

items.question: Does the paper show that vendor escalation with guaranteed support outperforms human audit? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The environment can run both protocols, but the paper deliberately draws no quantitative or protocol-ranking conclusions, because the protocols are simplified, the agents scripted and the configurations curated. It also stresses that no single protocol is a complete answer.
rubric: Answers not settled
Reasons that no quantitative or ranking conclusions are drawn from the simplified, curated synthetic run

items.question: Does the paper show that the C1–C4 classes are ordered by reversibility as well as by severity? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The case ranks the classes by severity only. The balancing framework's reversibility examples contrast a bounded, reversible single-transaction error with irreversible settlement failure or mass data exposure, but it never ranks C2 against C3 on reversibility.
rubric: Answers not settled
Reasons that the ordering is stated by severity and reversibility is only illustrated at the extremes, not ranked across all classes

items.question: Does the paper show that coalition arrangements such as shared audit consortia or South-South cooperation reduce deployers' oversight costs? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Coalition paths appear only as one consideration in a rubric that 'can' amortise oversight costs. The paper offers no evidence on their effect, and the cost proxy does not model them.
rubric: Answers not settled
Reasons that coalition paths are proposed as a consideration without supporting evidence or modelling

items.question: Does the paper show that AI control protocols provide no meaningful oversight for deployers without model access? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The paper treats output-level monitoring, defer-to-trusted routing, human audit and scope restriction as feasible without model access. Against a strong Position B, it argues that proportionate oversight, workflow design and incident management can do meaningful work, even if the assurance is partial.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Reasons that several protocols are feasible without model access and the paper argues proportionate oversight can do meaningful (if partial) work

items.question: Does the paper show that interpretability-supported auditing cannot become part of the Operator's oversight regime? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The Operator treats activation-level and interpretability-supported monitoring as longer-term possibilities. Their availability depends on the vendor's product roadmap and the Operator's interpretive capacity, rather than being ruled out.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Reasons that these are framed as longer-term possibilities contingent on the vendor roadmap and Operator capacity, not excluded

items.question: In an environment configuration with the pre-execution gateway present, would pairing it with the no-control protocol be expected to provide any prevention, and why?
items.answer: No. The gateway is only a review point between the agent's recommended action and mock execution, where the active protocol may hold, replace, escalate or pass the action. The no-control protocol accepts the agent's proposed action, so every recommendation passes through to execution. Prevention comes from what a protocol does at the gateway, not from the gateway alone.
rubric: Concludes that the gateway paired with no control gives no (or negligible) prevention.
Explains that the gateway is just a point where a protocol can hold, replace, escalate or pass actions, and that no control accepts or passes every proposed action.

items.question: The Operator's model risk function approves output-monitor thresholds at go-live. Under which model-version-control setting would those thresholds most likely stop being justified even if the monitor itself is unchanged, and why?
items.answer: Under the unpinned setting. There the vendor can change the underlying model on its own schedule, and the outputs being scored shift with it. A threshold calibrated on the validated model's outputs, with its implied flag and error behaviour, then no longer describes the model actually running, so it needs review and recalibration.
rubric: Identifies the unpinned setting, or equivalently vendor updates made without the deployer's involvement.

Explains that thresholds are calibrated against a specific model's outputs, so a changed model can invalidate the calibration (flag, false-positive or false-negative behaviour) even with the same monitor.

items.question: Under the coalition-paths consideration, several small operators share an audit consortium that reviews their flagged cases. Under what condition would this add little real oversight for a member operator, and why?
items.answer: It would add little when the member has no internal incident process, or no authority or capacity, to act on the consortium's findings. Acting means triage, scope narrowing, customer remediation and regulator notification. A flag has value only if the organisation can act on it, and the member stays accountable to its own regulator and board. A consortium spreads the cost of reviewing flags but cannot run the member's own incident management.
rubric: States the condition: the member lacks its own process, capacity or authority to act on what the consortium finds.

Explains with the distinction between monitoring and acting on monitoring, or with the fact that accountability and incident response stay with the member while the consortium only shares review cost.

items.question: Would the resampling protocol's protection hold against a C2 failure such as the stress scenario's slow elevation in hold recommendations for one merchant category, and why?
items.answer: Not reliably. Resampling works case by case: it picks the lowest-risk acceptable action among candidates for each individual action. A C2 failure is a pattern that only shows up across many cases, and each individual recommendation may look acceptable. The candidates also come from the same model and may share its bias. Catching C2 needs detection at the level of patterns or clusters.
rubric: Concludes that resampling would not reliably prevent or catch the C2 pattern.
Explains that resampling operates on individual actions or cases, while C2 is only visible as a pattern across many cases.

items.question: When would the Operator's data-residency rider provide no protection against a C3 event, and why?
items.answer: It gives no protection when protected data is exposed through tool calls or outputs, which is how the case defines C3. The rider only governs where data is stored, which is part of the infrastructure arrangement. It says nothing about what the model returns or which tools it calls. Mitigation for C3 lies in the interaction layer, through controlled tool interfaces, monitoring and editing of outputs.
rubric: States that the rider does not protect against exposure through outputs or tool calls (the case's C3 route).
Explains that the rider governs storage location (infrastructure) and not the interaction-layer behaviour through which C3 occurs.

items.question: The case suggests the control tax will be experienced as an extension of existing third-party and model risk budgets. For what kind of deployer would this expectation fail, and why?
items.answer: It would fail for deployers without established third-party and model risk governance, such as settings with less established oversight practice like parts of public administration or general enterprise. The expectation rests on the case's spend categories closely resembling costs already incurred to govern critical third-party technology services. Where that machinery does not exist, the costs would arrive as new budget lines rather than extensions of existing ones.
rubric: Identifies deployers lacking mature third-party and model risk management (for example, sectors with less established oversight practice).
Explains that the expectation depends on the oversight spend resembling existing third-party governance budgets, so without them the costs would be genuinely new.

items.question: Why does the case require that actions replaced under defer-to-trusted routing be recorded for later review?
items.answer: Post-incident review is central to regulated accountability: detection alone is not enough, and failures must also be explained. Without a record of what the model proposed and what replaced it, investigators could not reconstruct how a case was handled. They also could not check customer treatment or show validators and supervisors how the protocol behaved.
rubric: States that the records allow later reconstruction or diagnosis of what happened in the case.
Links this to regulated accountability, for example the distinction between detecting and explaining, audit and supervisory review, or checking customer treatment.

items.question: In the stress scenario, why must the Operator plan customer remediation even though the incident is a C2 pattern rather than a single incorrect hold?
items.answer: A C2 failure is made up of many incorrect individual hold decisions that spread across cases before detection, so each affected customer has suffered a C1-type harm. Narrowing scope and fixing the root cause stop further harm. They do not undo holds already placed on those customers.
rubric: States that the C2 pattern consists of many individual incorrect holds affecting real customers.
Explains that containment or root-cause fixes do not reverse holds already applied, so affected customers need separate remediation.

items.question: Why does the Operator weigh narrowing the assistant's scope for the affected merchant category in parallel with the vendor ticket, rather than waiting for the vendor's response?
items.answer: C2 errors keep spreading across cases until they are contained. The fix to the model is vendor-led, and its timing depends on the support terms. Scope narrowing falls within the Operator's own interaction layer, so it can halt further spread immediately. The Operator accepts lost usefulness, and more manual processing, while the investigation runs.
rubric: Explains that waiting would let the C2 pattern keep spreading because the model fix depends on the vendor and its timing.
Notes that scope narrowing is within the Operator's own control (operator-led interaction layer) and can act immediately, at a usefulness cost.

items.question: The environment's workflow is transaction-adjacent rather than settlement-operational. Why does it still include a C4 class?
items.answer: The case defines C4 as any action path that could disturb settlement, and even a dispute-triage workflow can make recommendations on settlement-critical cases. Synthetic cases therefore carry a settlement-critical marker, and such recommendations are labelled C4. This lets the environment represent the highest-severity class, and test controls such as excluding those paths, without connecting to settlement at all.
rubric: States that recommendations in a transaction-adjacent workflow can still touch settlement-critical cases, matching the case's definition of C4 as any action path that could disturb settlement.
Notes that C4 is a synthetic label (settlement-critical marker) that lets the highest-severity class and related controls be studied without real settlement access.

items.question: Why does the environment need the honest agent, given that AI control is concerned with worst-case behaviour?
items.answer: The honest agent provides a baseline of ordinary error. Against it, a protocol's effect on routine mistakes, and its costs during normal operation, can be seen. Those costs include false positives, audit load and lost task success. Regulated deployers judge controls on usefulness and cost as well as prevention, so they need to know how a protocol behaves when the model is not attacking.
rubric: States that the honest agent gives a baseline of ordinary error or routine operation.
Explains that this reveals protocols' costs under normal operation (false positives, audit burden, usefulness loss), which regulated deployers must weigh alongside worst-case safety.

items.question: Why does defer-to-trusted routing tend to carry a usefulness cost, beyond its workflow-design cost?
items.answer: Flagged actions are replaced by a weaker trusted model's output or a conservative fallback, which may be less accurate or helpful than the original. Some flags are false positives, and in those cases a good recommendation is swapped for a worse one. Safety is bought partly with usefulness.
rubric: Concludes that replacement can reduce task success or usefulness.
Explains that the replacement comes from a weaker or conservative trusted fallback, and that false-positive flags cause good recommendations to be replaced.

items.question: Why is it reasonable for the Operator to evaluate its controls against a worst-case untrusted model, even though its vendor is a commercial partner with no evident intent to harm it?
items.answer: AI control is designed for cases where a model's alignment cannot be verified, and the Operator has no model access: weights, architecture and activations are vendor-held. The vendor also holds private information under incomplete contracts, and verification is costly and asymmetric. The Operator therefore cannot confirm the model's behaviour directly, and planning for the worst case keeps its controls valid whatever the model's actual tendencies.
rubric: Concludes that worst-case evaluation is reasonable because the Operator cannot verify the model's alignment or behaviour.
Grounds this in the Operator's lack of model-layer access and/or the vendor's private information and costly, asymmetric verification.

items.question: A deployer with too few reviewers replaces human auditing of flagged cases with an AI auditor. Which practical consideration does this ease, and what does it bring in instead?
items.answer: It eases staffing and review capacity. The AI auditor, however, is another model, so it must be calibrated, documented, validated and justified to the model risk function, as an output monitor must be. Escalation paths are still needed. The cost shifts from staffing to validation rather than disappearing.
rubric: States that it eases the staffing or review-capacity consideration.
States that it introduces calibration, documentation and validation burdens (model risk justification) for the AI auditor, so cost shifts rather than disappears.

items.question: Which environment protocol and setting best represent the audit-and-attestation provisions in the Operator's contractual spend, and what part of that spend does the environment not capture?
items.answer: The vendor escalation protocol represents them: it requests vendor support for diagnosis or attestation. The vendor-support setting (none, delayed, guaranteed) stands in for what the contract secures. Usage appears as vendor-request count and vendor-assurance cost. The cost of negotiating and legally reviewing the provisions is an institutional friction the simulator does not model.
rubric: Identifies the vendor escalation protocol together with the vendor-support setting.
Notes that negotiation, legal review or procurement cost of the provisions is not captured by the simulator.

items.question: Of the case's four oversight spend categories, which has the weakest counterpart in the environment's decomposed cost proxy, and why?
items.answer: Contractual spend. Architectural spend maps to the logging, gateway and monitoring components. Capacity spend maps partly to human-audit cost. Scope decisions map to scope-restriction cost. Contractual spend, by contrast, means negotiating service, notification, audit and regulator-access terms, and the simulator does not model these procurement and legal frictions. Only per-request vendor-assurance cost touches it.
rubric: Identifies contractual spend.

Explains that the other categories have proxy components (logging, gateway, monitoring, human audit, scope-restriction cost), while contract negotiation and legal review are unmodelled institutional frictions.

items.question: Which decision in the stress scenario corresponds most closely to the environment's macro-shutdown protocol, and what cost does that decision carry?
items.answer: Narrowing the assistant's scope for the affected merchant category pending investigation. Like macro-shutdown, it puts a suspicious cluster into safe mode after repeated suspicious signals. Its cost is the usefulness lost for that whole category, which moves work into manual processing.
rubric: Identifies the decision to narrow scope for the affected merchant category (safe-moding the cluster).
States the cost as lost usefulness for the cluster, shifted to manual processing.

items.question: A supervisor wants evaluations to measure whether staff could explain a failure's root cause to the supervisor. How should a user adapt the environment, and what would it still fail to capture?
items.answer: The user should substitute a richer definition of diagnosis success. The environment's operationalisation is deliberately simple and designed to be replaced. Even so, the environment does not model human factors such as staff expertise or whether records are actually reviewed, and its data are synthetic. It still could not show whether real staff could explain a failure.
rubric: States that the user should replace the simple diagnosis-success definition with a richer one suited to the setting.
Notes that human factors (staff expertise, actual review) and real data remain unmodelled, so the result is still not a real-world estimate.

items.question: A payments operator plans to extend its assistant from dispute triage to directly initiating settlement adjustments. What does the paper's framework imply for oversight of that extension?
items.answer: The extension opens C4 action paths, which are the most severe and least reversible class, so it would justify the greatest oversight investment. It also removes the lever the case relies on, which is excluding C4-adjacent paths as a scope decision. That weakens what makes payments favourable terrain. Under the cost-versus-value consideration, the extension may not justify deployment at all.
rubric: Concludes that the extension would require much heavier oversight, or might not be justified at all.
Explains that it opens C4 (highest severity, least reversible) action paths and removes the scope-restriction lever of excluding C4-adjacent paths.

items.question: If oversight costs simply added up, with no design choice moving cost from one budget line to another, which evaluation recommendation would lose one of its stated motivations?
items.answer: It would weaken the warning that frameworks reporting only one cost category give a misleading impression of efficiency, which motivates reporting decomposed cost alongside the other dimensions. That warning rests on cost-shifting. Examples are scope narrowing lowering monitoring effort while raising manual processing, and vendor attestations lowering validation while raising contract management.
rubric: Identifies the recommendation against single-cost-category reporting, or in favour of decomposed or joint cost reporting.
Explains that it is motivated by costs shifting between lines (for example, scope narrowing raising manual processing, attestations raising contract management).

items.question: If vendor cooperation and supply terms were guaranteed never to change, which part of the paper's concession 'in support of both A and B' would lose force, and which part would remain?
items.answer: The part about arrangements that depend on vendor cooperation being subject to change would lose force; it backs Position B's fragility argument. The other part would remain: the assurance available to any single deployer is limited, which supports Position A, because the deployer still lacks model access and cannot verify the model directly.
rubric: Identifies that the point about vendor-dependent arrangements being subject to change (B's fragility argument) loses force.
States that the limited assurance available to a single deployer (supporting A) remains, because model access and verification are still absent.

items.question: If the four-pillar sovereignty formulation were a settled, peer-reviewed academic taxonomy, which hedge about the paper's four-layer typology would lose part of its stated basis?
items.answer: It would weaken the hedge that the typology is offered as a descriptive aid rather than a settled taxonomy. The paper bases that hedge partly on the sovereign-AI literature being fast-moving, partly non-peer-reviewed, and a policy and industry construct. The hedge would not vanish entirely, because the paper also modifies the framework by replacing the operational pillar with an interaction layer.
rubric: Identifies the hedge that the typology is a descriptive aid rather than a settled taxonomy.
Links that hedge to the source framework being a fast-moving, partly non-peer-reviewed policy and industry construct (optionally noting the paper's own modification still keeps it unsettled).

items.question: If the environment's human-audit reviewer had unlimited capacity, which practical consideration from the protocol table could the environment no longer represent?
items.answer: It could no longer represent staffing and escalation: review capacity that must be planned and resourced. With an unlimited reviewer, the human-audit protocol would no longer depend on audit budget and capacity limits. The environment would then miss the constraint the case links to capacity spend and to resourced escalation paths.
rubric: Identifies the staffing and escalation (review capacity) consideration for human auditing.
Explains that the capacity-limited reviewer is what makes audit budget and review resourcing matter in the environment.

items.question: If the environment's cost proxy omitted the scope-restriction cost component, how could the safety-usefulness-cost frontier mislead about the scope restriction protocol?
items.answer: Scope restriction would appear both safe and cheap, with a small cost marker. The usefulness given up by removing actions would be missing from its total control cost. This is the free-safety-gain impression that joint reporting is meant to prevent. The paper treats forgone usefulness as a real oversight cost; it appears as one of the case's spend categories.
rubric: States that scope restriction would look cheap or nearly costless as well as safe.
Explains that the forgone usefulness, which the paper treats as an oversight cost (scope decisions), would drop out of the cost total, encouraging the free-safety-gain reading.

items.question: If a regulated deployer could transfer accountability for a vendor model's behaviour entirely to the vendor, which central argument of the paper would lose support?
items.answer: The argument that control protocols become part of the deployer's wider oversight system, and that pricing the control tax requires attention to Layer 2 institutional embedding. That argument rests on the deployer staying accountable to its regulator, customers and board for a model it does not own. That accountability is what forces controls into its validation, audit and incident processes.
rubric: Identifies the Layer 2 / wider-oversight-system argument (pricing the control tax requires attention to institutional embedding).
Explains that it rests on the deployer remaining accountable to its regulator, board or customers despite not owning the model.

items.question: Would an LLM-in-the-loop version of the environment allow the paper to report sovereignty-discount estimates?
items.answer: No. Sovereignty discount refers to procurement, legal review, vendor-management and supervisory frictions that the simulator does not model at all. Swapping scripted agents for an LLM changes the agents' behaviour, not those institutional overheads.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that sovereignty discount consists of institutional frictions the simulator does not model, which agent realism does not add.

items.question: Would an LLM-in-the-loop version of the environment make its flag and false-positive rates more informative about monitor calibration?
items.answer: Yes. The scripted agents lack the ambiguity of real model outputs, which is exactly what monitor calibration must handle. An LLM in the loop would produce realistic outputs, so threshold, flag and false-positive results would bear more directly on calibration.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that scripted agents lack real output ambiguity, which monitor calibration depends on, and an LLM would supply it.

items.question: In the target-reachability template, would a profile meeting ≤1% failure and ≥75% usefulness for a given agent count as reaching the target even if its cost proxy were very high?
items.answer: Yes. The joint target is defined only by failure and usefulness thresholds, so cost does not enter whether a profile is counted. Cost has to be read separately, for example from the safety-usefulness-cost frontier.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that the target uses only failure and usefulness criteria, so cost is not part of reachability.

items.question: In the target-reachability template, would a profile that meets ≤1% failure and ≥75% usefulness against the honest agent thereby count as reaching the target for the stealthy access-aware agent?
items.answer: No. Reachability is computed and reported separately for each synthetic agent. The same profile can fail the target against the stealthy agent, which chooses lower-visibility failures when monitoring is weak.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that reachability is reported per agent, and that the stealthy agent's behaviour differs, so meeting the target for one agent does not carry over.

items.question: Would Position A's objection apply to a domestic deployer that runs a domestically built model whose behaviour it likewise cannot fully verify?
items.answer: Yes. Position A turns on verifiability: if the deployer cannot fully verify that a protocol works as intended, it should not count it as safety assurance. That concern does not depend on whether the model or supplier is foreign.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that Position A rests on verifiability, not on foreign dependency.

items.question: Would Position B's objection apply to a domestic deployer that runs a domestically built model on domestic compute under its own control?
items.answer: No. Position B objects to fragility from foreign dependency, where a vendor or state can revoke or change supply terms. Full-stack domestic capability is precisely the solution Position B endorses.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that Position B targets foreign-dependency fragility, and that domestic models, compute and control are what it calls for.

items.question: Under the balancing framework, would the availability of a regional regulatory college reduce the case for heavy oversight of a use case whose catastrophic action is severe and irreversible?
items.answer: No. The case for heavy oversight comes from the severity-and-reversibility consideration, which coalition availability does not change. Coalitions only change how the cost of oversight capability is shared.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that oversight need is driven by severity and reversibility, which coalition paths do not alter.

items.question: Under the balancing framework, would the availability of a regional regulatory college make heavy oversight of such a use case more affordable for an individual deployer?
items.answer: Yes. Coalition paths such as regional regulatory colleges amortise the cost of building oversight capability across multiple deployers. This lowers each deployer's share of the cost.
rubric: Answers yes.
Explains that coalitions spread the cost of oversight capability across multiple deployers.

items.question: Does the paper show that a configuration reaching its target-reachability threshold (≤1% failure and ≥75% usefulness) is the one a deployer should adopt? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The reachability table is a template, not findings, and is computed on synthetic data with scripted agents. The target also excludes cost, which the paper insists be reported together with prevention, diagnosis and usefulness. Meeting the target therefore says nothing about affordability or real-world suitability.
rubric: Answers not settled (or not supported).
Gives a reason: the target omits cost and/or diagnosis, and the table is a template on synthetic outputs rather than findings.

items.question: Does the paper show that an import-dependent regulated deployer such as the Operator has no sovereignty over its AI deployment? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The case access audit finds the Operator leads the interaction layer and shares the data and infrastructure layers, and is vendor-led only at the model layer. The framing treats sovereignty as distributed across layers, not binary.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites the access audit: interaction is operator-led, data and infrastructure are shared, only the model layer is vendor-led (sovereignty is partial or layered, not absent).

items.question: Does the paper show that the control tax is smaller for regulated deployers because existing third-party and model risk budgets absorb it? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper says the control tax is likely to be experienced as an extension of existing budgets, which describes where it appears rather than how large it is. It notes that costs tend to shift rather than disappear, and it produces no real cost estimates.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that being folded into existing budgets concerns where cost appears, not its size; costs shift rather than vanish, and no real cost estimates are given.

items.question: Does the paper show that bounded control gives the Operator adequate oversight of its dispute-triage deployment? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Position C is adopted only as a working frame, and the paper says its adequacy must be judged case by case according to severity. The case is illustrative and anonymised, and the simulation provides no real evidence of safety levels.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Gives a reason: Position C is a working frame whose adequacy is case by case, and the case and simulation are illustrative or synthetic rather than evidence.

items.question: Does the paper show, through its simulation, that control-protocol outputs feed effectively into a regulated deployer's incident-management procedures? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The simulator does not model human factors or institutional processes, so it cannot test integration with incident management. The paper's account of monitor flags flowing into triage, model risk review and vendor tickets comes from an illustrative stress scenario, not from measured results.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that the simulator omits human factors and institutional processes, and that the incident-management flow comes only from an illustrative scenario.

items.question: Does the paper show that weak supervisors cannot reliably oversee stronger AI systems? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper says it does not technically extend scalable oversight. It borrows only the structural observation that oversight capacity is a scarce resource whose adequacy can be analysed, and it makes no claim about whether weak-to-strong oversight succeeds.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that the paper only borrows the scarcity-of-oversight-capacity observation and does not test or extend scalable oversight.

rejected.question: Does the paper show that bounded control is adequate for regulated deployers in AI-importing jurisdictions? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
rejected.answer: Not settled. The paper adopts Position C only as a working frame. It says bounded control is a pragmatic position whose adequacy must be judged case by case according to severity. It concedes that the assurance any single deployer can obtain is limited and that vendor-dependent arrangements may change.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: Position C is a working frame whose adequacy is judged case by case; the paper concedes that assurance is limited.
